title: Monsoon Flight Cancellations in India: What Passengers Can Claim From Airlines
excerpt: DGCA rules entitle flyers to refunds, meals, hotel stays, and up to ₹10,000 in compensation — but weather disruptions complicate the picture. Here's what you're owed and how to get it.
body:
• DGCA rules require airlines to offer full refunds or alternate flights for any cancellation — but monetary compensation of up to ₹10,000 is waived when severe weather is the cause.
  • Even during monsoon-related cancellations, passengers are still entitled to meals, refreshments, hotel stays, and ground transport at the airline's expense.
  • New 2026 DGCA norms give all flyers a 48-hour free cancellation window on direct airline bookings and mandate refunds within 7 working days on credit cards.
  • Passengers can escalate unresolved complaints through the AirSewa portal, consumer courts, or — as a recent ₹1 lakh ruling against Vistara shows — the National Consumer Commission.

With the southwest monsoon in full swing, Indian airports are back in disruption mode. On July 5, Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport suspended all runway operations for an hour after gusty winds of up to 42 knots and heavy rain lashed the city. Seventeen flights were cancelled, 217 delayed, and 13 diverted to Ahmedabad, Surat, and Hyderabad. Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport diverted 15 flights on the same day. IndiGo, Akasa Air, Air India, and SpiceJet all issued travel advisories.

This pattern repeats every monsoon season — June through September — when heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, and low visibility push cancellations up by as much as 40 percent at India's busiest airports. For passengers, the question is always the same: what am I actually owed?

The Force Majeure Catch

India's passenger protection framework is governed by DGCA's Civil Aviation Requirement (CAR) Section 3, Series M, Part IV. Under these rules, if a flight is cancelled without at least 24 hours' notice, the airline must either rebook the passenger on an acceptable alternate flight or pay compensation on top of a full refund.

The compensation is tiered by block time: up to ₹5,000 for flights of one hour or less, ₹7,500 for flights between one and two hours, and ₹10,000 for flights over two hours. For denied boarding — common during monsoon when airlines consolidate partially empty flights — penalties are steeper: 200 percent of the one-way base fare plus fuel surcharge (capped at ₹10,000) if an alternate departs within 24 hours, and 400 percent (capped at ₹20,000) if it takes longer.

"Under the same CAR, airlines must still provide meals and refreshments proportional to waiting time once a delay crosses two hours for short-haul flights and four hours for long-haul."

The catch: airlines are explicitly exempt from paying monetary compensation when a cancellation results from "extraordinary circumstances" beyond their control, including meteorological conditions and Air Traffic Control decisions. Severe monsoon weather qualifies. This means the ₹5,000-to-₹10,000 payout for cancellations — and the denied boarding penalties — can legally be withheld when rain is the documented cause.

What Airlines Still Owe You

The force majeure exemption covers cash compensation only. Under the same CAR, airlines must still provide meals and refreshments proportional to waiting time once a delay crosses two hours for short-haul flights and four hours for long-haul. If a delay runs overnight — or exceeds 24 hours — the airline must arrange hotel accommodation and ground transfers at no cost.

For cancellations of any kind, the airline must offer either a full ticket refund or rebooking on the next available flight. Under updated 2026 DGCA norms effective March 26, credit card refunds must now be processed within 7 working days. Bookings through travel agents carry a 14-working-day deadline. Cash purchases at airline offices must be refunded immediately.

A separate 2026 rule introduced a 48-hour "look-in" window: passengers who book directly through an airline's website can cancel or amend tickets within 48 hours of booking at no additional charge, provided the domestic flight is at least 7 days away or an international flight is 15 days away.

How to File a Claim

The DGCA's escalation pathway is straightforward. Start by contacting the airline directly — each carrier is required to appoint a nodal officer and appellate authority for passenger grievances. File within 30 days of the disruption, and keep boarding passes, booking confirmations, and receipts for any out-of-pocket expenses.

If the airline's response is unsatisfactory, file a complaint on the government's AirSewa portal or app. The platform tracks complaints and requires airlines to respond within a set timeframe. For disputes above ₹20,000 or cases of deficient service, consumer courts remain an option. In July 2026, the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission awarded ₹1 lakh to a passenger against Vistara for last-minute cancellation due to overbooking — a reminder that regulatory protections have real teeth, according to a Bar and Bench report.

What NRIs Flying to India Should Know

For diaspora travellers booking international flights to India, the DGCA's rules apply to all carriers — domestic and foreign — operating to and from Indian airports. A 2026 directive requires foreign airlines to appoint local representatives in India and maintain formal grievance mechanisms registered on the DGCA's e-Governance portal.

However, India's compensation regime differs from the EU's EC 261 framework, which allows claims of up to €600 regardless of weather. In India, force majeure wipes out monetary compensation entirely — though care obligations (meals, hotels, transfers) remain intact. Passengers on connecting itineraries that include a domestic leg should note that the DGCA rules govern the Indian segment even if the international leg falls under a different regulatory regime.

Travel Insurance and Practical Tips

With monetary compensation off the table during genuine weather disruptions, travel insurance becomes the main financial backstop. Policies that explicitly cover weather-related trip interruptions can reimburse additional accommodation, meals, and rebooking costs that airlines won't cover.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation disclosed in a Rajya Sabha reply in February 2026 that IndiGo alone spent ₹22.68 crore on passenger compensation and facilitation during December 2025 disruptions. Airlines do pay when they must — the challenge for passengers is knowing when the rules apply and documenting the claim. Keep your boarding pass, photograph the delay board, save every receipt, and file early.
